title: 3-2-1, How to Start a New Habit, the Power of Responsibility, and Prioritizing the Long-Term
author: James Clear
summary: Clear's weekly 3-2-1 issue collects three of his own aphorisms, two borrowed quotations and a single closing question, and the through line is the gap between what a person can do at their peak and what they can sustain. The habit idea is the sharpest: he argues most people choose a new habit by asking what they could manage on a good day, when the useful question is what survives a bad one. The second idea compresses a whole investing debate into a two line distinction between building wealth and keeping it. The third and longest claim is that improvement in health, relationships and work follows an increase in responsibility rather than motivation, so a change in trajectory usually requires taking ownership of something new. The borrowed quotations set money against time, with Murakami drawing the line between what money can and cannot buy. The issue closes on a one line prompt rather than a prescription. For the archive its value is as a compact statement of Clear's position that durable change is a matter of scale and ownership rather than intensity.
points: Clear inverts the usual habit question, arguing the right test is not what a person can do on their best days but what they can stick to on their worst.
He compresses an investing distinction into two lines, holding that concentration produces wealth while diversification protects it.
The longest idea ties any positive change in trajectory to an increase in responsibility, naming health, relationships and starting a business as instances of the same pattern.
The two borrowed quotations both concern allocation, with Murakami separating what money can buy from what only time can, and Berry arguing for planting what the planter will not live to harvest.
quotes: When choosing a new habit many people seem to ask themselves, "What can I do on my best days?
The trick is to ask, "What can I stick to even on my worst days?
Start small. Master the art of showing up. Scale up when you have the time, energy, and interest.
Concentration produces wealth. Diversification protects wealth.
Life rarely changes in a positive way without an increase in responsibility.
This is true in many areas: taking ownership of your health, committing to a relationship, starting a business, etc.
Whatever it is, if you want the trajectory to change, the amount of responsibility usually has to change.
Spend your money on the things money can buy. Spend your time on the things money can't buy.
